topic: En route altitudes, airways and holding

notes.front: What is a Victor airway?
notes.back: A VOR airway, identified by “V” (Victor) and a number and charted in black; outside Alaska it is based solely on VOR aids.
notes.explanation: The letter and number are how you name the airway in a flight plan and on the chart.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-4, “Airways and Route Systems”
notes.evidence: Except in Alaska, the VOR airways are: predicated solely on VOR or VORTAC navigation aids; depicted in black on aeronautical charts; and identified by a “V” (Victor) followed by the airway number (for example, V12).
notes.example: Like a numbered road between towns, but in the sky and built from VOR radials.

notes.front: What is a T-route?
notes.back: A low-altitude area navigation route for aircraft equipped with GPS or GPS/WAAS, charted on the low altitude en route charts.
notes.explanation: Only aircraft with suitable GPS equipment may use it.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-4, “Airways and Route Systems”
notes.evidence: T-routes are available for use by GPS or GPS/WAAS equipped aircraft from 1,200 feet above the surface (or in some instances higher) up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL. T-routes are depicted on Enroute Low Altitude Charts.
notes.example: Like a cycle path marked only on a satnav, but for aircraft flying on GPS.

notes.front: What is the minimum en route altitude (MEA)?
notes.back: The lowest published altitude between radio fixes that assures navigation signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance requirements.
notes.explanation: It is published for each airway or route segment between the fixes that define it.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-35
notes.evidence: The MEA is the lowest published altitude between radio
notes.example: Like the lowest safe water depth marked for a shipping lane, but also promising that the lane's beacons can be received.

notes.front: What is the minimum obstruction clearance altitude (MOCA)?
notes.back: The lowest published altitude between fixes that meets obstacle clearance for the whole route segment.
notes.explanation: It assures acceptable navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: acceptable navigational signal coverage only within 22 NM
notes.example: Like the MEA with the promise of good reception taken away far from the beacon.

notes.front: What is the minimum reception altitude (MRA)?
notes.back: The lowest altitude at which an intersection can be identified; it is published for a fix only when it is higher than the MEA.
notes.explanation: FAA flight inspection sets it by finding where the navigation signals can be received.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-35
notes.evidence: for the fix and is the lowest altitude at which an intersection
notes.example: Like the lowest floor of a building where your phone still picks up two masts, but for fixing an intersection.

notes.front: What is the minimum crossing altitude (MCA)?
notes.back: The lowest altitude at which certain fixes must be crossed when flying towards a higher minimum en route IFR altitude.
notes.explanation: It is published where obstacles would stop a normal climb to the higher MEA after the fix.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “Minimum Crossing Altitude (MCA)”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: An MCA is the lowest altitude at certain fixes at which the
notes.example: Like a sign saying you must already be at the top of the ramp before the bridge, not climbing onto it.

notes.front: What is the maximum authorized altitude (MAA)?
notes.back: The highest usable altitude or flight level on a route segment at which adequate reception of navigation signals is assured.
notes.explanation: Above it, signal reception is no longer assured, for example because of frequency interference.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: which adequate reception of navigation signals is assured.
notes.example: Like a height limit on a road bridge, but set by radio reception rather than clearance.

notes.front: What is a minimum turning altitude (MTA)?
notes.back: A higher minimum altitude for turning at certain fixes, where the MEA may not give enough obstacle clearance in the turn.
notes.explanation: The need comes from the higher airspeeds flown at 10,000 feet MSL or above, which widen the turn.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-7, “Minimum Turning Altitude (MTA)”
notes.evidence: Due to increased airspeeds at 10,000 ft MSL or above, the published minimum enroute altitude (MEA) may not be sufficient for obstacle clearance when a turn is required over a fix, NAVAID, or waypoint.
notes.example: Like a road with a lower speed limit only on the sharp bend, but raising the minimum height instead.

notes.front: What is a changeover point (COP)?
notes.back: The point on a route segment between two navigation aids where you switch from the station behind to the station ahead.
notes.explanation: It marks where navigation guidance should change over from one facility to the next.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-6, “Changeover Points (COPs)”
notes.evidence: The COP is a point along the route or airway segment between two adjacent navigation facilities or waypoints where changeover in navigation guidance should occur. At this point, the pilot should change navigation receiver frequency from the station behind the aircraft to the station ahead.
notes.example: Like the midpoint of a long tunnel where your radio swaps from one relay transmitter to the next.

notes.front: What is an off-route obstruction clearance altitude (OROCA)?
notes.back: A published altitude giving 1,000 feet of terrain and obstruction clearance (2,000 in designated mountainous areas), off published routes.
notes.explanation: It is published for situational awareness, flight planning and contingency use.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-9, “VFR/IFR Flights”
notes.evidence: OROCA is a published altitude which provides 1,000 feet of terrain and obstruction clearance in the US (2,000 feet of clearance in designated mountainous areas).
notes.example: Like the maximum elevation figure on a VFR chart, but with an obstruction clearance margin added for IFR use.

notes.front: What is the minimum vectoring altitude (MVA)?
notes.back: The altitude at or above which ATC radar-vectors IFR aircraft, apart from certain authorised procedures.
notes.explanation: Exceptions include radar approaches, radar departures and special VFR.
notes.evidence: Except where authorized for radar approaches, radar departures, special VFR, or when operating in accordance with vectors below minimum altitude procedures, vector IFR aircraft at or above minimum vectoring altitudes.
notes.example: Like a crane operator's minimum lift height over a building site, but set for ATC's radar vectors.

notes.front: What is an expect further clearance time (EFC)?
notes.back: The time at which a pilot can expect to receive clearance beyond a clearance limit.
notes.explanation: It tells a holding pilot when onward clearance should come.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), glossary, “Expect-further-clearance (EFC)”, p. G-7
notes.evidence: expect to receive clearance beyond a clearance limit.
notes.example: Like the “next train expected at” board on a platform, but for leaving a holding pattern.

notes.front: Between what altitudes are VOR airways designated?
notes.back: From 1,200 feet above the surface (sometimes higher) up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: These are the airways charted on the IFR en route low altitude charts.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-4, “Airways and Route Systems”
notes.evidence: The VOR and L/MF (nondirectional radio beacons) Airway System consists of airways designated from 1,200 feet above the surface (or in some instances higher) up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL. These airways are depicted on IFR Enroute Low Altitude Charts.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
uses: IFR en route low altitude chart

notes.front: Under § 91.181, where must you fly on an airway under IFR in controlled airspace, unless ATC authorises otherwise?
notes.back: Along the centreline of the airway.
notes.explanation: On other routes the rule asks for the direct course between the navigation aids or fixes that define the route.
notes.evidence: (a) On an ATS route, along the centerline of that airway. (b) On any other route, along the direct course between the navigational aids or fixes defining that route.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At a course change on an airway, what does the FAA expect pilots to do to stay within the airway?
notes.back: Lead the turn, and take other actions they consider necessary.
notes.explanation: The expectation covers any action pilots consider necessary to stay as close as possible to the airway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-5, “Airway or Route Course Changes”
notes.evidence: Consequently, the FAA expects pilots to lead turns and take other actions they consider necessary during course changes to adhere as closely as possible to the airways or route being flown.

notes.front: Over what width of an airway does its MEA apply?
notes.back: The entire width of the airway, segment or route between the radio fixes that define it.
notes.explanation: The MEA is not tied to the centreline alone but covers the whole width of the segment.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-35
notes.evidence: entire width of the airway, segment, or route between the

notes.front: On an IFR flight plan cleared to maintain VFR conditions on top, may you fly below the minimum en route IFR altitudes?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Minimum altitude rules apply to all IFR flights, in IFR or VFR weather, assigned an altitude or VFR-on-top.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-35
notes.evidence: conditions on top, pilots may not fly below minimum en

notes.front: Where both an MEA and a MOCA are published, when may you fly below the MEA down to the MOCA using a VOR?
notes.back: When the navigation signals are available and you are within 22 NM of that VOR.
notes.explanation: The pilot's reasonable estimate of the distance is what counts.
notes.evidence: However, if both a MEA and a MOCA are prescribed for a particular route or route segment, a person may operate an aircraft below the MEA down to, but not below, the MOCA, provided the applicable navigation signals are available. For aircraft using VOR for navigation, this applies only when the aircraft is within 22 nautical miles of that VOR
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When must a climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude begin?
notes.back: Immediately after passing the point beyond which that higher minimum applies.
notes.explanation: If obstructions intervene, the MCA sets a higher altitude at which to cross that point instead.
notes.evidence: Climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude shall begin immediately after passing the point beyond which that minimum altitude applies, except that when ground obstructions intervene, the point beyond which that higher minimum altitude applies shall be crossed at or above the applicable MCA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When ground obstructions intervene, how must you cross the point where a higher minimum IFR altitude begins?
notes.back: At or above the applicable MCA.
notes.explanation: Where no obstructions intervene, the climb simply starts immediately after that point.
notes.evidence: except that when ground obstructions intervene, the point beyond which that higher minimum altitude applies shall be crossed at or above the applicable MCA.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where an MTA applies, from where to where must you be at or above it?
notes.back: From no later than the turn point until you join the centreline of the route after the turn.
notes.explanation: Once established on that centreline, the MEA or MOCA again sets the minimum altitude available.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-7, “Minimum Turning Altitude (MTA)”
notes.evidence: When an MTA is applicable for the intended route of flight, pilots must ensure they are at or above the charted MTA not later than the turn point and maintain at or above the MTA until joining the centerline of the ATS route following the turn point.

notes.front: Where is a changeover point normally located, and when is it charted?
notes.back: Midway between the facilities on a straight segment; it is charted, with mileages, when not midway.
notes.explanation: On a dogleg segment it sits where the radials or courses forming the dogleg intersect.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-6, “Changeover Points (COPs)”
notes.evidence: The COP is normally located midway between the navigation facilities for straight route segments, or at the intersection of radials or courses forming a dogleg in the case of dogleg route segments. When the COP is NOT located at the midway point, aeronautical charts will depict the COP location and give the mileage to the radio aids.

notes.front: Is an OROCA assessed for navigation signal, radar or communications coverage?
notes.back: No. It is published for situational awareness, flight planning and in-flight contingency use.
notes.explanation: It gives terrain clearance only, so it is not a guarantee that you can navigate or talk to ATC there.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-9, “VFR/IFR Flights”
notes.evidence: These altitudes are not assessed for NAVAID signal coverage, air traffic control surveillance, or communications coverage, and are published for general situational awareness, flight planning and in-flight contingency use.

notes.front: Can an MVA be lower than the MEA or MOCA charted for the same place?
notes.back: Yes. Some MVAs may be lower than MEAs, MOCAs or other charted minimum altitudes.
notes.explanation: The handbook says only that some may be lower, so check rather than assume.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “Minimum Vectoring Altitudes (MVA)”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: some MVAs may be lower than MEAs, MOCAs, or other

notes.front: Which way do you turn in a standard holding pattern?
notes.back: Right turns. A nonstandard pattern uses left turns.
notes.explanation: ATC states the direction of turn only when left turns are to be made or it considers it necessary.
notes.evidence: Standard Pattern. Right turns (See FIG 5-3-3.) Nonstandard Pattern. Left turns

notes.front: In a clearance to hold at an uncharted fix, how is the direction of holding from the fix given?
notes.back: As one of the eight cardinal compass points, such as north, northeast or east.
notes.explanation: It is the first item ATC includes when the pattern is not charted.
notes.evidence: Direction of holding from the fix in terms of the eight cardinal compass points (i.e., N, NE, E, SE, etc.).

notes.front: In an uncharted holding clearance, when is leg length given in miles?
notes.back: When DME or area navigation is to be used.
notes.explanation: Leg length in minutes is given on pilot request or when the controller thinks it necessary.
notes.evidence: Leg length in miles if DME or RNAV is to be used (leg length will be specified in minutes on pilot request or if the controller considers it necessary).

notes.front: The holding pattern is charted on your route. What may ATC reduce the holding instructions to?
notes.back: The charted holding direction and “as published”, for example “hold east as published”.
notes.explanation: ATC must still give complete holding instructions whenever you ask for them.
notes.evidence: When the pattern is charted on the assigned procedure or route being flown, ATC may omit all holding instructions except the charted holding direction and the statement AS PUBLISHED; for example, HOLD EAST AS PUBLISHED. ATC must always issue complete holding instructions when pilots request them.

notes.front: When cleared to a fix short of the destination with delay expected, what must ATC issue?
notes.back: Complete holding instructions (unless the pattern is charted), an EFC and its best estimate of further delay.
notes.explanation: The FAA places this responsibility on ATC, not the pilot.
notes.evidence: Whenever an aircraft is cleared to a fix other than the destination airport and delay is expected, it is the responsibility of ATC to issue complete holding instructions (unless the pattern is charted), an EFC time and best estimate of any additional en route/terminal delay.

notes.front: Approaching a clearance limit with no charted pattern and no holding instructions, what should you do?
notes.back: Ask ATC for holding instructions before reaching the fix.
notes.explanation: Asking first removes the chance of entering a pattern other than the one ATC wants.
notes.evidence: If no holding pattern is charted and holding instructions have not been issued, the pilot should ask ATC for holding instructions prior to reaching the fix. This procedure will eliminate the possibility of an aircraft entering a holding pattern other than that desired by ATC.

notes.front: What is the maximum holding airspeed from the minimum holding altitude up to 6,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: 200 knots indicated airspeed.
notes.explanation: The limits rise with altitude: 230 knots from 6,001 to 14,000 feet, and 265 knots above.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the maximum holding airspeed from 6,001 to 14,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: 230 knots indicated airspeed.
notes.explanation: Some patterns in this band are restricted to 210 knots, shown by an icon on the chart.
notes.evidence: MHA - 6,000' 200 6,001' - 14,000' 230 14,001' and above 265 NOTE- These are the maximum indicated air speeds applicable to all holding. The following are exceptions to the maximum holding airspeeds: Holding patterns from 6,001' to 14,000' may be restricted to a maximum airspeed of 210 KIAS.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the maximum holding airspeed at 14,001 feet MSL and above?
notes.back: 265 knots indicated airspeed.
notes.explanation: These maximums apply to all holding unless a lower speed is charted.
notes.evidence: 14,001' and above 265 NOTE- These are the maximum indicated air speeds applicable to all holding.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With no clearance beyond the fix, when should you begin slowing to the maximum holding airspeed?
notes.back: When 3 minutes or less from the clearance limit.
notes.explanation: The aim is to cross the fix initially at or below the maximum holding airspeed.
notes.evidence: When an aircraft is 3 minutes or less from a clearance limit and a clearance beyond the fix has not been received, the pilot is expected to start a speed reduction so that the aircraft will cross the fix, initially, at or below the maximum holding airspeed.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which holding entry flies outbound parallel to the holding course on the non-holding side for one minute?
notes.back: The parallel entry.
notes.explanation: You then turn in the direction of holding through more than 180° and return to the fix or intercept the inbound course.
notes.evidence: the parallel entry procedure would be to turn to a heading to parallel the holding course outbound on the nonholding side for one minute, turn in the direction of the holding pattern through more than 180 degrees, and return to the holding fix or intercept the holding course inbound.

notes.front: Which holding entry turns outbound on the holding side to a heading 30° off the course, for one minute?
notes.back: The teardrop entry.
notes.explanation: You then turn in the direction of holding to intercept the inbound holding course.
notes.evidence: the teardrop entry procedure would be to fly to the fix, turn outbound to a heading for a 30 degree teardrop entry within the pattern (on the holding side) for a period of one minute, then turn in the direction of the holding pattern to intercept the inbound holding course.

notes.front: Which holding entry simply flies to the fix and turns to follow the pattern?
notes.back: The direct entry.
notes.explanation: It is the entry for arrivals from the sector the FAA labels (c) in its entry diagram.
notes.evidence: Direct Entry Procedure. When approaching the holding fix from anywhere in sector (c), the direct entry procedure would be to fly directly to the fix and turn to follow the holding pattern.

notes.front: At or below 14,000 feet MSL, how long should the inbound leg of a holding pattern take?
notes.back: 1 minute.
notes.explanation: The first outbound leg is flown for the same time, then adjusted to give the right inbound time.
notes.evidence: Inbound Leg. At or below 14,000 feet MSL: 1 minute. Above 14,000 feet MSL: 11/2 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Above 14,000 feet MSL, how long should the inbound leg of a holding pattern take?
notes.back: 1½ minutes.
notes.explanation: The longer leg applies to the higher-altitude band only.
notes.evidence: Above 14,000 feet MSL: 11/2 minutes. NOTE- The initial outbound leg should be flown for 1 minute or 1 1/2 minutes (appropriate to altitude).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When does timing of the outbound leg begin?
notes.back: Over or abeam the fix, whichever occurs later.
notes.explanation: If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when the turn outbound is completed.
notes.evidence: Outbound leg timing begins over/abeam the fix, whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when turn to outbound is completed.

notes.front: In holding, how much drift correction should you use on the outbound leg compared with the inbound leg?
notes.back: Three times the inbound correction, applied the other way.
notes.explanation: Tripling it outbound avoids major turning adjustments.
notes.evidence: Compensate for wind effect primarily by drift correction on the inbound and outbound legs. When outbound, triple the inbound drift correction to avoid major turning adjustments

notes.front: Without area navigation guidance, at what rate or bank should you make turns in holding?
notes.back: 3° per second, 30° of bank, or 25° with a flight director, whichever needs the least bank.
notes.explanation: These limits apply to the entry as well as the pattern itself.
notes.evidence: For holding not involving the use of RNAV lateral guidance, make all turns during entry and while holding at: 3 degrees per second, or 30 degree bank angle, or 25 degree bank angle, provided a flight director system is used. NOTE- Use whichever requires the least bank angle.

notes.front: What two reports should you make about a holding fix or clearance limit?
notes.back: The time and altitude on reaching it, and when leaving it.
notes.explanation: Together they tell ATC when you arrived at the limit and when you left it.
notes.evidence: Pilots should report to ATC the time and altitude/flight level at which the aircraft reaches the clearance limit and report leaving the clearance limit.

notes.front: Holding at a VOR, when should you begin the turn to the outbound leg?
notes.back: At the first complete reversal of the TO/FROM indicator.
notes.explanation: That reversal marks station passage over the fix.
notes.evidence: When holding at a VOR station, pilots should begin the turn to the outbound leg at the time of the first complete reversal of the to/from indicator.

notes.front: Which holding instructions should include an EFC?
notes.back: All of them.
notes.explanation: The EFC also gives a definite time to leave the fix if radio contact is lost.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “Holding Procedures”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: holding instructions should include an EFC time. In the

notes.front: If two-way radio communication is lost while holding, what does the EFC let you do?
notes.back: Depart the holding fix at a definite time.
notes.explanation: Plan the last lap of the pattern so as to leave the fix as close as possible to that time.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “Holding Procedures”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: allows the pilot to depart the holding fix at a definite time.

notes.front: A segment has an MEA of 6,000 and a MOCA of 4,500 feet. Navigating by VOR, you are 30 NM from the station. May you descend to 5,000 feet?
notes.back: No. Below the MEA you may use the MOCA only within 22 NM of the VOR.
notes.explanation: Beyond 22 NM the MOCA does not assure the signal, so the MEA remains your minimum.
notes.evidence: For aircraft using VOR for navigation, this applies only when the aircraft is within 22 nautical miles of that VOR
notes.choices:
A) Yes, 5,000 is above the MOCA
B) No, not beyond 22 NM of the VOR
C) Yes, if ATC is not told
D) Only in VFR conditions
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the 22 NM limit. C: telling ATC or not does not change the rule. D: the MOCA rule has no VFR exception.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At the next fix the MEA rises from 5,000 to 8,000 feet, and no MCA is shown. When do you start climbing?
notes.back: Immediately after passing the fix where the 8,000-foot minimum begins.
notes.explanation: With no MCA published, the rule asks for the climb to start right after that point.
notes.evidence: Climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude shall begin immediately after passing the point beyond which that minimum altitude applies
notes.choices:
A) Immediately after passing the fix
B) 5 NM before the fix
C) Whenever convenient on the next segment
D) Only when ATC tells you
notes.choicesExplained: B: no rule sets a distance before the fix; even a charted MCA only sets the altitude at which to cross the fix. C delays the climb the rule makes immediate. D: the minimum altitude is yours to meet.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying a Victor airway between two VORs 80 NM apart, with no changeover point charted, where should you retune to the station ahead?
notes.back: About 40 NM along, at the midway point.
notes.explanation: A changeover point that is not midway is charted, so no symbol means midway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-6, “Changeover Points (COPs)”
notes.evidence: The COP is normally located midway between the navigation facilities for straight route segments
notes.choices:
A) At the first station
B) At the midway point
C) When the first needle wanders
D) At the second station
notes.choicesExplained: A and D leave you on the wrong station for half the segment. C waits for guidance to degrade, which the changeover point exists to prevent.

notes.front: You plan to cruise at FL 210 on VOR-based routes. Which route system will you be flying on?
notes.back: The jet route system: Victor airways stop below 18,000 feet MSL, and jet routes run from 18,000 feet MSL to FL 450.
notes.explanation: The jet route system runs from 18,000 feet MSL to FL 450.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-4, “Airways and Route Systems”
notes.evidence: The jet route system consists of jet routes established from 18,000 feet MSL to FL 450 inclusive.
notes.choices:
A) Victor airway
B) Jet route
C) T-route
D) Off-airway route only
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are low-altitude systems below 18,000 feet MSL. D: there is a published high-altitude system for VOR routes.

notes.front: At 180 knots you reach a VOR where the airway turns 60°. Starting the turn over the station would carry you wide. What does the FAA expect?
notes.back: Lead the turn, starting it before the fix so as to stay within the airway.
notes.explanation: Turns begun at or after fix passage may exceed the airway or route boundaries.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-5, “Airway or Route Course Changes”
notes.evidence: Turns which begin at or after fix passage may exceed airway or route boundaries.
notes.choices:
A) Turn only after station passage
B) Lead the turn
C) Ask ATC for vectors every time
D) Fly past, then cut back
notes.choicesExplained: A and D may take you outside the airway. C is not required; leading the turn is the pilot's job.

notes.front: Flying VFR-on-top on an IFR flight plan, you see a smooth cloud top 500 feet below the MEA and want to cruise just above it. Allowed?
notes.back: No. You may not fly below the minimum en route IFR altitude.
notes.explanation: Minimum IFR altitudes still apply to a VFR-on-top flight.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-35
notes.evidence: conditions on top, pilots may not fly below minimum en
notes.choices:
A) Yes, you are VFR
B) No, not below the MEA
C) Yes, if you are VFR-on-top above a layer
D) Only below 18,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat VFR-on-top as VFR flight, but the minimum IFR altitudes still apply. D: altitude band makes no difference.

notes.front: ATC says: “Hold west of the Mayfield VOR on the 270 radial, expect further clearance at 1520.” No turn direction is given. Which way do you turn?
notes.back: Right: it is a standard pattern.
notes.explanation: ATC names the direction of turn only when left turns are to be made or it considers it necessary.
notes.evidence: Direction of turn if left turns are to be made, the pilot requests, or the controller considers it necessary.
notes.choices:
A) Right turns
B) Left turns
C) Either, at your choice
D) Ask ATC; the clearance is incomplete
notes.choicesExplained: B would have been stated. C: the standard pattern is fixed. D: nothing is missing, since right turns need not be stated.

notes.front: You are told to hold at 10,000 feet. No speed is charted for the hold. What is your maximum holding airspeed?
notes.back: 230 knots indicated airspeed.
notes.explanation: 10,000 feet falls in the 6,001 to 14,000-foot band.
notes.choices:
A) 200 knots
B) 230 knots
C) 265 knots
D) 175 knots
notes.choicesExplained: A is the limit up to 6,000 feet. C applies above 14,000 feet. D applies only where charted.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You are holding at 16,000 feet MSL. What inbound leg time should you aim for?
notes.back: 1½ minutes.
notes.explanation: Above 14,000 feet MSL the inbound leg is 1½ minutes rather than 1.
notes.evidence: Above 14,000 feet MSL: 11/2 minutes.
notes.choices:
A) 1 minute
B) 1½ minutes
C) 2 minutes
D) Whatever the outbound leg took
notes.choicesExplained: A applies at or below 14,000 feet. C is not a standard time. D: the inbound time is fixed; the outbound is adjusted.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Inbound in a hold, you need 5° of left correction to track the course. What correction do you apply outbound?
notes.back: 15° to the right.
notes.explanation: Triple the inbound drift correction on the outbound leg, applied to the opposite side.
notes.evidence: for example, if correcting left by 8 degrees when inbound, correct right by 24 degrees when outbound.
notes.choices:
A) 5° right
B) 10° right
C) 15° right
D) 15° left
notes.choicesExplained: A and B under-correct. D is on the wrong side: outbound the wind acts from the other side of the aircraft.

notes.front: An entry takes you to the fix, then outbound on the holding side at a 30° angle for one minute, then back to the inbound course. Which entry is it?
notes.back: The teardrop entry.
notes.explanation: The parallel entry goes outbound on the non-holding side, and the direct entry turns straight into the pattern.
notes.evidence: turn outbound to a heading for a 30 degree teardrop entry within the pattern (on the holding side) for a period of one minute
notes.choices:
A) Direct
B) Parallel
C) Teardrop
D) Procedure turn
notes.choicesExplained: A turns straight into the pattern. B flies outbound on the non-holding side. D is a course reversal, not a holding entry.

notes.front: You are holding with an EFC of 1540 when your radios fail. When should you plan to leave the holding fix?
notes.back: As close as possible to 1540.
notes.explanation: The EFC gives a definite time to depart the fix after lost communication, so you plan the last lap to meet it.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “Holding Procedures”, p. 2-51
notes.evidence: allows the pilot to depart the holding fix at a definite time.
notes.choices:
A) At once
B) As close as possible to 1540
C) When fuel reaches minimum fuel
D) Only when ATC calls
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the time given. C is not how the EFC works. D cannot happen with the radios failed.

notes.front: What does an MEA assure that a MOCA does not, away from the VOR?
notes.back: Acceptable navigation signal coverage; the MOCA assures it only within 22 NM of the VOR.
notes.explanation: Both meet obstacle clearance requirements for the segment.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 2, “IFR En Route Altitudes”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: acceptable navigational signal coverage only within 22 NM
